## Bois & Chiffons — Marketing strategy (internal)

Notes: every factual statement below is grounded in the brand website pages cited in sourceUrls. Customer segments and positioning are treated as hypotheses to validate.

## Executive summary

- Bois & Chiffons presents itself as a direct-to-consumer (DTC) furniture brand emphasising solid wood, design and durability (site headlines: “Meubles en bois design | Mobilier élégant et durable”; product filters show “Bois Massif”, “Bois d’acacia”, “Bois de manguier”, etc.) [see source].
- The catalogue is broad (site shows 1,391 products in the “all products” collection) and organised by home room + wood type, supporting both consumer and professional use cases (the homepage explicitly links to “Architectes et décorateurs”, “Professionnels de l'immobilier”, “Bureaux professionnels”, “Hôteliers et restaurateurs”).

## Positioning (hypothesis — validate)

- Hypothesis: Positioned as a design-forward solid-wood furniture brand that trades on craftsmanship, natural materials and a French lifestyle aesthetic (“L'Art de Vivre à la Française”) rather than mass, low-cost furniture. Evidence: homepage copy and footer tags referencing “Bois Massif”, “Matières Naturelles”, “Fabrication Artisanale” and the tagline “L'Art de Vivre à la Française”.
- Hypothesis: Offers both retail and professional (B2B) services — the site includes a “Request a quote” link and dedicated pages for professionals (architects, hospitality, property professionals). Validate demand and processes. [see source]

## Target customer segments (hypotheses to validate)

List of candidate segments suggested by the site content — each needs quantitative validation (traffic, conversion, AOV, LTV):

1. Design-conscious homeowners / apartment owners
   - Rationale: product photography, curated collections (e.g., Kfir, Bunting, Forest), large living/bedroom/dining ranges indicate consumer interiors use. [see source]
2. Mid-to-upper price buyers seeking durable, natural-material furniture
   - Rationale: emphasis on solid wood and artisanal manufacture; product pages show full-priced and sale-priced items (e.g., multiple “Sale-50%” examples on bed pages) — pricing tier needs confirmation. [see source]
3. Trade / professional buyers (B2B)
   - Rationale: explicit pages/links for architects, real estate professionals, hotels & restaurants and a “Request a quote” CTA. [see source]
4. International shoppers (multi-region & multi-currency site)
   - Rationale: Country/region switcher lists many countries (France, Belgium, Germany, India, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, etc.). Validate which markets drive revenue. [see source]
5. Small contract/hospitality buyers (hotels, restaurants)
   - Rationale: site mentions professional hospitality and offers a quote request flow—validate throughput and margin. [see source]

## Value proposition (what to test)

- Core claim: handcrafted, solid-wood furniture with an emphasis on design, durability and natural materials.
  - Source evidence: homepage and product pages with wood-type filters and labels (“Bois Massif”, “Bois d’acacia”, “Bois de manguier”), and site tags “Fabrication Artisanale”.
- Secondary claim: wide choice and curated collections that help customers build a cohesive interior.
  - Evidence: organised collections (Kfir, Bunting, Forest, Maya, etc.) and room-based navigation (Salon, Chambre, Salle à manger). [see source]
- B2B proposition: tailored professional selections and quotes (explicit “Request a quote” and professional pages). [see source]

Why customers would care (hypotheses):
- Durability and natural-material look/feel vs cheaper engineered furniture — test through customer interviews and returns/complaints analysis.
- One-stop shop for timber furniture in multiple woods and styles — test by measuring cross-sell and basket composition.

## Key differentiators (supported by the site)

- Large, wood-focused assortment (site lists 1,391 products in the full catalogue). [see source]
- Clear emphasis on specific woods (acacia, mango, oak, pine, recycled wood) visible in navigation and “Buy by wood” filters. [see source]
- B2B support (architects, hospitality) alongside consumer retail — shown by dedicated CTAs. [see source]
- Multi-country, multilingual storefront and social presence (site includes country selector and links to Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, X, YouTube). [see source]

## Seasonal moments & commercial rhythms (hypotheses to validate)

Evidence on the site suggests the following moments worth exploring and validating with data:

- New collection launches / “Dernières nouveautés” — site highlights “Dernières nouveautés” and “L'Art de Vivre à la Française 2026”. Validate cadence of new drops and their conversion impact. [see source]
- Promotional sale windows — site shows a visible promotion (“10 % de réduction supplémentaire sur tous les articles en promotion | Code : SALE10”) and product pages show sale badges (e.g., “Sale-50%” on several bed SKUs). Validate timing and margin impact of promotions. [see source]
- Room refresh seasons (spring/summer or autumn) — hypothesis only (site structure by room suggests seasonally-driven buying). Validate via historical order data and traffic trends. [see source]
- B2B procurement cycles — hospitality and real estate projects often have project-tied timelines. Validate by reviewing B2B quote request frequency and project start/end timelines. [see source]

## Channels the brand appears to use (observed)

- Owned commerce channel: website with full product catalogue and checkout. Evidence: ecommerce cart and product lists. [see source]
- Social platforms (linked): Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, X (Twitter), YouTube. These appear in the header/footer as active social links. Validate channel performance and content mix. [see source]
- B2B sales channel: quote request form and dedicated professional pages (architects, hospitality, property professionals). [see source]
- Email / newsletter: site shows newsletter subscription CTA (“Abonnez-vous à notre newsletter”). Validate email database size & performance. [see source]

Unknown / not visible on site (gaps — confirm with the team):
- Paid acquisition channels in use (search, social ads, marketplaces) — Unknown — confirm with the team.
- CRM / ESP platform and segmentation approach — Unknown — confirm with the team.
- Organic SEO vs paid traffic split and top-performing landing pages — Unknown — confirm with the team.

## Key metrics & goals worth validating (recommended tests & KPIs)

These are suggested objectives and the data you should pull to validate / prioritise them.

1. Commercial goals to validate
   - Conversion rate (site-wide and by country / collection) — Unknown — confirm with analytics.
   - Average order value (AOV) by channel & product category — Unknown — confirm with sales data.
   - Gross margin by category and during promotions (e.g., items showing 50% sale) — Unknown — confirm with finance.
   - Repeat purchase / customer retention (CLTV) — Unknown — confirm with CRM.
   - B2B quote-to-order conversion rate and average project size — Unknown — confirm with sales team.
   - Review score target: current visible aggregated rating is 4.33 (1,766 reviews) — validate distribution, product-level NPS and opportunities for improvement. [see source]

2. Audience & acquisition goals to validate
   - Top-performing geographies (traffic & revenue) given multi-country site — Unknown — confirm with analytics.
   - Channel ROI (organic, paid search, social organic & paid, email) — Unknown — confirm with ad platforms & analytics.
   - Social engagement -> website conversion (which platform drives best commerce outcomes) — Unknown — confirm with UTM and platform analytics.

3. Product & assortment goals to validate
   - High-opportunity SKUs and collections (top sellers and highest margin) — Unknown — confirm with sales reports.
   - Stockouts / availability impact on conversion (site shows some out-of-stock counts) — Unknown — confirm with inventory data.

4. Customer experience goals to validate
   - Checkout abandonment rate and drivers (shipping cost, lead time) — Unknown — confirm with analytics and checkout funnel data.
   - Returns rate and reasons — Unknown — confirm with operations.
   - Delivery lead times and premium delivery offering performance (site references “Livraison Premium”) — Unknown — confirm with operations/policies. [see source]

## Quick tactical recommendations (first 90-day test plan)

1. Measurement & diagnostics (day 0–30)
   - Confirm analytics setup and extract core KPIs by country/collection/channel: traffic, conversion, AOV, revenue, returns.
   - Pull B2B pipeline metrics: quote requests, conversion to order, average order value.
   - Audit social channel performance (Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, X, YouTube) and capture referral traffic to product pages.

2. Low-risk experiments (day 30–90)
   - Test promotional messaging lift: run a targeted campaign (email + social organic) highlighting a curated “new collection” and compare conversion vs control; measure margin impact given visible existing promo code. [site shows promo code SALE10].
   - Improve B2B capture: simplify the quote form CTA and A/B test landing copy tied to hospitality / architects to increase qualified leads.
   - On-site merchandising: promote best-selling, high-margin wood categories on homepage and room pages; measure click-throughs and conversion.

3. Validate seasonal calendar
   - Establish cadence of product launches and historical promotion windows (holiday, summer, collection drops). Use this to plan two major campaigns in the next 12 months: a collection launch and a sale event. (Site indicates active “Dernières nouveautés” and promotions; confirm historical dates.)

- Which countries drive most revenue and highest conversion? (analytics)
- What is the typical AOV and margin by wood type or collection? (ERP/finance)
- What are the top 10 best-selling SKUs and their stock status? (inventory)

## Competitor analysis — Bois & Chiffons (internal)

Purpose: a concise, evidence-based scan of likely competitors and reference brands in the European/online solid-wood furniture market; each entry lists public positioning signals, observable strengths (public signals) and suggested lessons/hypotheses for Bois & Chiffons to validate.

Context (Bois & Chiffons public signals)

- Brand signals from the site: positioned on wooden furniture with emphasis on design, quality and durability; multiple solid-wood species (mango, acacia, oak, pine, recycled wood) and extensive collections; sells both to consumers and to professionals (architects, hoteliers, B2B quote offering). Source pages: Bois & Chiffons homepage and Collections pages.  
  (Source pages: https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en , https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections , https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/all). 

Competitors & reference brands (public signals, strengths, lessons)

1) Tikamoon — France / solid‑wood specialist

- Positioning (public signal): marketed as a design-forward brand specialising in solid wood furniture and "slow furniture"; emphasises material selection and durability; operates online with physical showrooms in France. ([tikamoon.com](https://www.tikamoon.com/?utm_source=openai))
- Strengths (public signals): recognized for solid‑wood focus and storytelling about craftsmanship and sustainability; presence across channels (e‑commerce + boutiques); media coverage positions it as a higher‑end, slow‑furniture option. ([tikamoon.com](https://www.tikamoon.com/ins-la-marque-tikamoon-353.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Lessons / hypotheses to validate for Bois & Chiffons:
  - Emphasise a clear “slow furniture” value proposition and practical content (care, finishes, provenance) to differentiate from mass-market players. (Hypothesis — validate with A/B content tests and audience interviews.)
  - Explore a small network of experience centres or pop‑ups to let customers touch wood finishes and learn maintenance — Tikamoon’s boutiques are a public signal of this strategy. ([tikamoon.com](https://www.tikamoon.com/ins-nos-boutiques-257.htm?utm_source=openai))

2) Maisons du Monde — large French multi‑category retailer

- Positioning (public signal): broad home and décor player positioning itself as "inspiring, accessible and sustainable" with large omnichannel reach (many stores + online). ([corporate.maisonsdumonde.com](https://corporate.maisonsdumonde.com/en/about-us?utm_source=openai))
- Strengths (public signals): scale (extensive retail footprint in Europe), wide style coverage and mass-market accessibility; strong brand awareness in France/Europe. Recent press notes point to business volatility in market context (public news reporting). ([fr.wikipedia.org](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maisons_du_Monde?utm_source=openai))
- Lessons / hypotheses to validate for Bois & Chiffons:
  - Maisons du Monde’s scale advantage is not a template to copy but indicates opportunity: target a clear niche (solid‑wood / artisan / design) rather than compete on breadth/price. (Hypothesis — test messaging that contrasts craftsmanship vs mass assortment.)
  - Monitor pricing/promotions from mass players and protect perceived value with clearer provenance and aftercare services.

3) Ethnicraft — European solid‑wood designer (higher-end)

- Positioning (public signal): positions on timeless design, handcrafted solid wood and durability; targets residential and contract projects and emphasizes authenticity and sustainability in materials. ([inspiration.ethnicraft.com](https://inspiration.ethnicraft.com/hubfs/2.%20WEBSITE%20CATALOGUES/Commercial%20catalogue.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Strengths (public signals): strong design credentials and reputation in contract/residential projects; clear premium positioning around solid wood and craftsmanship. ([cdn.uc.assets.prezly.com](https://cdn.uc.assets.prezly.com/5b64b043-9203-469c-817d-edeb5b6548a4/-/inline/no/ethnicraft-corporate-press-kit-2018.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Lessons / hypotheses to validate for Bois & Chiffons:
  - Learn from Ethnicraft’s emphasis on project / contract credentials: develop clearer case studies or a dedicated trade channel to win hospitality/real‑estate business (Bois & Chiffons already has B2B signals — validate expanding this). (Hypothesis — field test a hospitality-focused catalogue and landing page.)
  - Strengthen design storytelling (e.g., designer narratives, material origin) to support premium pricing.

4) Kave Home — omnichannel design brand (Iberia origin, expanding)

- Positioning (public signal): a global, design-driven brand with omnichannel presence; recent repositioning messaging emphasises permanence and resisting fast furniture trends. ([archdaily.com](https://www.archdaily.com/catalog/en/companies/5471/kave-home?utm_source=openai))
- Strengths (public signals): international footprint, strong digital commerce and marketing, campaigns that articulate brand values (e.g., “Here to Stay” anti‑fast‑furniture stance). ([es.linkedin.com](https://es.linkedin.com/posts/nara-camps-valls-50704b25_en-kave-home-lanzamos-nuevo-posicionamiento-activity-7369330243687399424-Sr8Q?utm_source=openai))
- Lessons / hypotheses to validate for Bois & Chiffons:
  - Consider a concise brand narrative that contrasts permanence and timber quality vs fast furniture — test this in digital channels. (Hypothesis — message experiments on homepage and paid ads.)
  - Kave’s omnichannel growth underlines the value of coordinated online/offline experiences; evaluate whether limited showrooms, partner galleries or shop‑in‑shop trials make sense for Bois & Chiffons’ markets.

5) Bolia — Scandinavian design brand with emphasis on sustainable materials

- Positioning (public signal): Scandinavian design, nature-inspired aesthetics and use of responsibly‑sourced wood (FSC referenced in public materials). ([hicontract.com](https://www.hicontract.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/EN_The_Journal_by_BOLIA.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Strengths (public signals): design-driven collections, emphasis on responsible sourcing and craftsmanship; structured creative lookbooks and brandbooks supporting premium perception. ([feats.co](https://www.feats.co/project/brandbook?utm_source=openai))
- Lessons / hypotheses to validate for Bois & Chiffons:
  - Make sustainability credentials clearer and specific (e.g., Forest certifications, traceability) as public signals matter — audit current claims and decide what to publish. (Gap — confirm Bois & Chiffons’ certifications.)
  - Use high‑quality lookbooks / lifestyle imagery to lift perceived value for mid‑premium ranges.

6) West Elm (Williams‑Sonoma) — international contemporary design retailer

- Positioning (public signal): contemporary, accessible modern design backed by a major parent company; emphasizes design collaborations and sustainability initiatives in marketing. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Elm?utm_source=openai))
- Strengths (public signals): scale and design collaborations, strong marketing and product breadth; reputation for contemporary styling and frequent product drops/collaborations. ([homesandgardens.com](https://www.homesandgardens.com/decor/pierce-and-ward-west-elm-new-collection?utm_source=openai))
- Lessons / hypotheses to validate for Bois & Chiffons:
  - Consider limited collaborations / capsule collections (with designers or artisans) to create PR moments and justify premium pricing. (Hypothesis — pilot a small capsule with a named designer.)
  - Beware of customer service/quality reputation pitfalls seen in public commentary for large players — use after‑sales and visible guarantees as differentiators.

7) Made.com — design‑oriented online retailer (status and relevance)

- Positioning (public signal): historically a digital-first design brand aiming to democratise higher‑end design; brand ownership and availability shifted after administration events (public record). Recent editorial/commercial collaborations continue. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made.com?utm_source=openai))
- Strengths (public signals): design credibility and history of high‑profile collaborations; brand recognition among ecommerce design shoppers. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made.com?utm_source=openai))
- Lessons / hypotheses to validate for Bois & Chiffons:
  - Watch how heritage digital brands reconfigure after financial stress — there can be opportunities to capture disaffected customers if Bois & Chiffons communicates reliability and stock/lead‑time transparency.

Actionable takeaways (short list)

- Clarify Bois & Chiffons’ primary positioning hypothesis: "design-led solid wood with artisanal finish + B2B capability" vs simply "large assortment of wood furniture." Use the homepage language and collections as starting point but run a one-week homepage messaging test that contrasts "craftsmanship/provenance" vs "wide selection/price." ## Brand Voice — Bois & Chiffons (internal guidance)

This document summarises the voice, tone and language patterns that currently appear on boisetchiffons.fr (English storefront). All statements are grounded in the site pages listed below. Use this as a working brief — treat suggested customer segments and positioning as hypotheses to validate with customer data and the commercial team.

## Core personality (what the site communicates)
- Warmly refined: the site repeatedly uses evocative, lifestyle-forward phrases (e.g. “Faites de votre maison votre plus belle destination”; “L'Art de Vivre à la Française”) that position the brand as aspirational and tasteful rather than mass-market. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Craft & natural materials focus: the site foregrounds wood types, artisanal construction and natural materials (e.g. “Bois Massif”, “Matières Naturelles”, “Fabrication Artisanale”, product lines described as “bois de manguier massif”, “bois d’acacia”). This signals a craft-led, material-first brand voice. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en, https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/all]
- Design and durability: product copy and meta text emphasise design quality and longevity (e.g. “Meubles en bois design | Mobilier élégant et durable”, “design, qualité et durabilité”). Use of the words “élégant”, “durable” and “design” recurs across pages. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Inspirational / editorial tone: sections such as “Bois Vivant. Des Espaces Qui Respirent.” and the blog-like headings (“5 meilleurs bois…”, “La commode sculptée…”) show a content-led, inspirational voice for lifestyle and education. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Professional & trade-ready cues: there are dedicated calls for architects, decorators and hospitality (“Architectes et décorateurs”, “Hôteliers et restaurateurs”, “Request a quote”), indicating B2C and B2B audiences and a voice that must be credible to professionals. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Tone — short guidance
- Primary tone: warm, refined, confident — avoid brash salesiness.
- Secondary tones to use as needed: informative/educational for product details; practical and straightforward for logistics (shipping, returns); professional for trade / B2B communications.
- Avoid: gimmicky, slangy, hyper-casual or discount-first language as the brand presents itself as craft-led and design-focused. Evidence: product descriptions and hero lines emphasise craft/durability over price messaging. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Vocabulary and language to prefer
(derived from site language and phrase patterns)
- Words/phrases to use often: wood, solid wood (bois massif), handcrafted / artisanal, design, elegant / élégance, durable / long-lasting, natural materials, collection, silhouette, finish, texture, crafted, signature, French art de vivre / L'Art de Vivre
  - Examples taken from the site: “Meubles en bois design | Mobilier élégant et durable”, “Silhouettes sculpturales façonnées en bois de manguier massif”, “Bois Massif”, “Matières Naturelles”, “Fabrication Artisanale”. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Descriptive adjectives to prefer: warm, sculptural, organic, timeless, refined, crafted, natural
- Use sensory language for materials: grain, texture, finish, patina — the site uses tactile, material-forward descriptions (e.g. “Textures organiques”, “Bois Vivant”). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Words and tones to avoid
- Avoid discount-first or bargain-heavy phrasing as the homepage emphasises craft and design rather than price. (While the site shows sales, the brand language is not discount-led.) [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Avoid terms that imply cheap mass-production (e.g., “mass-produced”, “plastic”, “cheap”) — these conflict with “bois massif” and “fabrication artisanale” positioning. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en, https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/all]
- Avoid unverified sustainability claims (e.g., “certified carbon-neutral”, “100% FSC-certified”) unless the legal/compliance team provides specific certification evidence. The site has a “Durabilité” section but does not show specific certification badges on the pages we reviewed. Mark such claims as Unknown — confirm with the team. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Languages to use and how
- Site languages available: English, Français, Português (Portugal). The storefront shows a language menu with these options; however, much on the English path remains in French. Use both English and French content intentionally depending on audience and channel; don’t mix languages unintentionally in the same sentence. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Tone differences: when writing in English, preserve the refined and slightly formal register that the French copy uses (e.g., translate “L'Art de Vivre à la Française” as an evocative phrase rather than a literal, blunt translation). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Hypothesis to validate: which language is primary per market (e.g., France vs international). Unknown — confirm with the team. (Listed in gaps.)

## Sentence style and structure
- Prefer short to medium-length sentences: many headings and product titles are compact and descriptive (“Tables”, “Buffets et bahuts”, “Silhouettes sculpturales…”) which creates a clean, magazine-like reading rhythm. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Use active voice and descriptive noun phrases: e.g., “Silhouettes sculpturales façonnées en bois de manguier massif” — sculptural noun phrases foreground design. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Use present tense for product descriptions and aspirational copy (e.g., “Aménager Tous les Secteurs avec Style”). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- For practical information (shipping, returns, availability), use concise, factual sentences that answer customer questions quickly. The site has separate pages for returns, shipping and product attributes. Follow that separation in copy. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Example phrasings taken from the site (use as approved in tone and register)
- “Faites de votre maison votre plus belle destination” — high-level brand hero line (French). Use as-is for French marketing; for English use an evocative equivalent, keeping the aspirational register (e.g., “Make your home your most beautiful destination”). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- “L'Art de Vivre à la Française” — evocative positioning line; use as a cultural touchpoint rather than literal claim. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- “Meubles en bois design | Mobilier élégant et durable” — succinct product/category line emphasising design + durability. Use similar triplets in headlines: material + design + benefit. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- “Silhouettes sculpturales façonnées en bois de manguier massif.” — material-forward, sculptural phrasing. Use the same structure: visual quality + material + method. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- “Bois Vivant. Des Espaces Qui Respirent.” — short, poetic sentence fragments that imply life and warmth in interiors. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Topics and approaches that seem off-brand
- Hard discounting and bargain-led creative: while the site shows promotions, the overall editorial voice is craft/design-led; marketing that foregrounds “cheap” or bargain-hunting risks diluting perceived quality. Evidence: emphasis on “fabrication artisanale”, materials and collections. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Overly technical manufacturing jargon for consumer-facing pages: the brand language is tactile and design-led rather than highly technical. Leave deep technical specs for product pages or trade documentation. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/all]
- Trend-chasing ephemeral messaging (“hot trends”, “viral look”) — the site leans toward timeless, material-focused positioning (e.g., “timeless”, “élégant”). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Casual/slang tone (e.g., “epic deal”, “OMG”) — inconsistent with the refined, material-led voice on site. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Hypotheses (to validate with research / analytics)
- Hypothesis: primary consumers are design-conscious homeowners seeking durable, natural-material furniture. Evidence: product language emphasises design, materials and “timeless” appeal, and collections are curated by wood type and style. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en, https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/all]
- Hypothesis: second audience is trade (architects, hotels, restaurants) — site explicitly has sections for “Architectes et décorateurs” and “Hôteliers et restaurateurs”. Voice should have a slightly more technical and businesslike register in B2B materials. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Hypothesis: multicultural/international positioning (language selector + country/region list). Validate which markets (France vs UK, EU, India) receive localized copy and how tone should shift by market. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Practical copy guidelines (do/don't)
- Do: lead with the material and design benefit (e.g., “Sculpted mango wood headboard — warm, tactile presence in the bedroom”). Mirror structure used across the site. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en, https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/lits]
- Do: use sensory descriptors for wood and finishes; keep sentences concise in headings and slightly longer in product descriptions. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Do: separate inspirational (homepage, editorial) and transactional copy (product pages, shipping info). The site already separates editorial lines from product details and logistics. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Don’t: make unconfirmed sustainability certification claims; check legal/CSR team before using terms like “certified” beyond what the site states. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Tone decisions by channel (recommendation)
- Homepage / hero: poetic, aspirational, short fragments drawn from the site (“Bois Vivant. Des Espaces Qui Respirent.”). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Product pages: factual + sensory; list materials first, then benefits (durability, finish). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/all]
- Email promotions: respectful and design-led; if discounts are mentioned, frame them as limited or curated rather than a race to the lowest price (site shows promo codes but overall voice is not discount-first). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- B2B / trade comms: professional, service-oriented — mirror the site’s trade pages and “Request a quote” language. [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Example 'on-brand' copy snippets (English equivalents inspired by site tone)
- Hero: “Make your home your most beautiful destination.” (based on “Faites de votre maison votre plus belle destination”). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Product header: “Sculptural mango-wood silhouette — crafted for warmth and longevity.” (based on “Silhouettes sculpturales façonnées en bois de manguier massif”). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]
- Category intro: “Furniture designed to create harmony in every corner of the home.” (based on “Mobilier conçu pour créer une harmonie dans chaque coin de la maison.”). [https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en]

## Topics to escalate / check with teams (gaps)
- Target customer profiles (detailed personas and primary markets). Unknown — confirm with the team.
- Official stance and documented copy policy for French phrases on the English site (when to keep French, approved French taglines to retain untranslated). Unknown — confirm with the team.
- List of verified sustainability claims and certifications the brand may use in copy (FSC, PEFC, carbon, etc.). Unknown — confirm with the team.
- Legal/compliance do’s and don’ts for claims about durability, origin and sourcing. Unknown — confirm with legal.
- Tone preferences for B2B materials vs B2C across markets (is B2B tone expected to be markedly different?). Unknown — confirm with sales/trade team.
- Official word list or forbidden terms maintained by the brand (if any). Unknown — confirm with brand team.

## Sources
- Main storefront (hero, language menu, claim lines, editorial headings, navigation): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en
- Collections index (site organisation, category language patterns): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections
- Products listing / all products (material and product taxonomy, “bois manguier”, “bois acacia” listings): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/all
- Beds collection (example product phrasing and price layout): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/lits
- Salon collection (category language and product counts): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/salon
- Poufs collection (example category copy and product counts): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/poufs


## Next steps (recommended)
- Validate the hypotheses and gaps with commerce, legal and CSR teams (see Gaps above).
- Create a short bilingual (EN/FR) mini style guide with 10 on-brand headline templates and 10 product-description sentence templates based on the examples above.
- Test 3 A/B hero lines in English copy that retain the brand’s French cultural cues to measure conversion and brand perception across markets.

## Content strategy — Bois & Chiffons (proposal to validate)

Note: all items below are proposals to validate with testing and internal confirmation. Statements marked as hypotheses should be treated as assumptions to validate with analytics, customer research and the product/team.

---

## Evidence base (pages reviewed)
- Homepage / brand overview: https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en
- Collections index and browse: https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections
- Full product listing (counts / filters): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/all

- Living room collection (product mix / category examples): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/salon
- Poufs collection (product examples / small-collection size): https://www.boisetchiffons.fr/en/collections/poufs

---

## Strategic context (grounded observations)
- Brand proposition on site: emphasis on solid wood furniture, design and durability (phrases on homepage such as "Meubles en bois design | Mobilier élégant et durable", and categories like "Bois Massif" / "Matières Naturelles" / "Fabrication Artisanale"). [Source: homepage]
- Product breadth: site lists many collections and woods (acacia, mango, oak, pine, recycled wood) and categories across home (living, dining, bedroom, entry/office). [Sources: homepage; collections; collections/all]
- Product scale: catalog listing shows "1391 products" (site search/filter). [Source: collections/all]
- B2B focus: site includes dedicated pages/links for "Architectes et décorateurs", "Professionnels de l'immobilier" and hospitality ("Are you furnishing a hotel or restaurant? Receive your professional selection and quote."). This indicates an active B2B channel to validate. [Source: homepage]
- Social proof: homepage displays a rating "4.33 ★ (1766)" — useful for social proof content. [Source: homepage]
- Content resources on site: blog excerpts/headlines appear on homepage (e.g. "De la bûche au salon : mobilier en bois massif ...", "5 meilleurs bois pour un meuble bois massif : g...") indicating editorial / storytelling assets exist or are planned. [Source: homepage]
- Promotional mechanics present on site (sales codes shown, example: SALE10). Useful to link promotional content to commerce. [Source: homepage]

---

## Proposed high-level content pillars (to validate)
(Each pillar ties to site content and to buyer needs. Treat segments and priorities as hypotheses.)

1) Craftsmanship & Materials (product trust)
- Why: site emphasizes "Bois Massif", specific woods (acacia, mango), "Fabrication Artisanale". Use to build credibility.
- Example topics: wood origins & characteristics, close-ups of joinery/finishes, "behind the piece" maker stories.

2) Home inspiration & Styling (inspiration -> consideration)
- Why: large catalog across rooms and lifestyle language such as "Faites de votre maison votre plus belle destination" and prominent collections. Use visual inspiration to drive discovery and saves.
- Example topics: room moodboards, mix-and-match with collections (Bunting, Kfir, Forest, etc.), seasonal styling.

3) Product education & specs (conversion)
- Why: complex purchases (large furniture) require clear dimensions, materials, delivery and care information. Site shows detailed filters and dimensions in listings.
- Example topics: product walkthroughs, how to measure for a table/bed, materials comparison (acacia vs mango), durability claims.

4) Sustainability & Commitments (trust / differentiation)
- Why: site includes a "Durabilité"/"Nos engagements" menu and mentions natural materials — customers likely care about origin and impact.
- Example topics: supply chain transparency, longevity / care guidance, recycling / end-of-life.

5) Customer stories & social proof (trust / retention)
- Why: rating on homepage and "Aimé par nos clients" section. Use real homes and reviews to reduce friction.
- Example topics: customer room photos, testimonials, before/after installs, UGC showcases.

6) B2B & Trade (lead generation for professionals)
- Why: explicit site sections for architects / hotels / real estate and a "Request a quote" CTA for projects.
- Example topics: case studies (hotel / restaurant fits), specification sheets, project pricing workflows.

7) Offers & Product News (activation)
- Why: site displays promotions (promo code) and many product launches/collections. Use to drive urgency and visits.
- Example topics: new collection reveals, limited-time discounts, clearance highlights.

---

## Audience hypotheses (to validate)
- H1: Design-conscious homeowners who want durable, natural materials and warm interiors. [Supported by home-facing language and collections] [Source: homepage]
- H2: Trade professionals (architects, interior designers, estate/hospitality buyers) who need catalogs, specs and quotes. [Supported by dedicated pages and B2B CTA] [Source: homepage]
- H3: Inspiration seekers using Pinterest/Instagram to discover room ideas and save products. [Supported by strong visual catalog and Pinterest/Instagram icons on the site] [Source: homepage]

Treat these as hypotheses to validate via analytics, CRM, and ad audience data.

---

## Channel-by-channel formats & proposals (to validate)
Note: format suggestions map to user intent and platform best practices; prioritize repurposing studio product photography + lifestyle shoots + short video.

Instagram (visual discovery & engagement)
- Formats to test:
  - Reels (short product storytelling: materials, assembly, scale in a room)
  - Carousel posts (hero product + detail shots + dimensions/specs card)
  - Instagram Shopping product tags (catalog integration) — proposal to confirm availability
  - UGC reposts / customer rooms (with permission)
  - Stories: sale timers, poll about finishes, swipe-up / link stickers to collection pages
  - Guides (curated collections: "Living room essentials", "Bedroom: wooden beds")
- Rationale: visual-first audience; use short video for higher organic reach and carousels for product detail.
- Primary CTAs to test: "View collection", "Shop this look", "Save for later", "Request a quote" (for B2B lead capture)
- Tie back to site: collections, product pages and newsletter CTA. [Source: homepage; collections]

Facebook (consideration & commerce)
- Formats to test:
  - Product catalog ads / shoppable posts linking to collection/product pages
  - Long-form video: 60–120s product walkthroughs / maker interviews
  - Event/pop-up announcements (special sales, collection drops)
  - Customer review posts and collection highlights
- Primary CTAs: "Shop now", "Request a quote", "Sign up for newsletter"
- Rationale: mixes commerce and community; use for retargeting and conversions. [Source: homepage — promo and newsletter]

Pinterest (discovery & planning)
- Formats to test:
  - High-resolution lifestyle Pins (room setups) linking to collection or product pages
  - Product Rich Pins (product metadata, price, availability) — proposal to confirm integration
  - Idea pins (step-by-step styling guides, moodboards)
  - Collections / boards per room style (e.g., "Scandi-warm living rooms with Bunting")
- Primary CTAs: "Save to board", "See product" (drive to product/collection)
- Rationale: strong top-of-funnel planner audience for furniture purchases. [Source: homepage; collections — many room categories]

LinkedIn (B2B / employer branding)
- Formats to test:
  - Case studies & project spotlights (hotel / restaurant / office installs) with measurable outcomes
  - Thought leadership posts on sustainable materials and supply chain
  - Job posts / employer brand content ("Careers" link on site indicates hiring page)
  - Product specheets & downloadable catalogs for trade
- Primary CTAs: "Request a quote", "Download project spec", "Contact our trade team"
- Rationale: site explicitly targets architects, hospitality and real-estate professionals; LinkedIn is efficient for trade leads. [Source: homepage]

Cross-channel production note
- Source assets from: product photography, lifestyle shoots, maker/interior videos, customer UGC, editorial blog posts (site has content headlines). Use modular edits for each platform.
- Confirm whether product feed/shop integrations (Instagram Shopping, Pinterest Rich Pins, Facebook Catalog) are configured. Unknown — confirm with the team.

---

## Suggested content mix (sample weekly split — proposal to validate with analytics)
- 35% Inspiration & styling (high-quality lifestyle images, moodboards) — drives saves & discovery
- 25% Product education & specs (walkthroughs, dimension cards, material explainers) — aids consideration
- 15% Craftsmanship & sustainability stories (maker profiles, material sourcing) — builds differentiation
- 15% Social proof & UGC (customer photos, review highlights) — reduces purchase friction
- 10% Promotions / News (new collections, sales, B2B offers) — drives conversions

Note: percentages are starting hypotheses to test; adjust per channel performance and pipeline goals.

---

## Hook ideas (short headline prompts to test)
(Use A/B tests — keep copy short on social)
- "Warm wood, timeless design — see the Bunting living collection." [ties to collection names on site] [Source: homepage]
- "From log to living room: how our pieces are made." [echoes blog headline on homepage "De la bûche au salon"] [Source: homepage]
- "Which wood fits your home? Acacia vs Mango — quick guide." [ties to woods listed on site] [Source: homepage; collections/all]
- "Design that lasts: meet our handcrafted tables." [ties to "Fabrication Artisanale" on site] [Source: homepage]
- "Spec-ready furniture for projects — request a trade quote." [ties to B2B CTA on site] [Source: homepage]

Test hooks in short-form video intros, pin titles and paid creatives.

---

## CTA recommendations (to validate by funnel stage)
- Discovery / Inspiration: "Save this look" / "View collection" / "Explore styles"
- Consideration / Product pages: "Check dimensions" / "See materials" / "Add to cart" / "Request a quote" (for large or trade purchases)
- Conversion / Offers: "Shop sale — apply code SALE10" (code visible on homepage) / "Limited-time offer — shop now" [Source: homepage]
- B2B / Trade: "Request a quote" / "Get the trade catalog" / "Book a consultation" [Source: homepage]
- Retention / CRM: "Sign up for newsletter" (newsletter prompt on homepage) / "Share your room (tag us)" [Source: homepage]

---

## Short editorial calendar example (first 2 weeks — proposal)
Week 1
- Mon (Instagram Reel): "From log to living room" — 30s maker + material close-ups -> CTA: view collection [Source: homepage]
- Wed (Pinterest): Room moodboard pin "Warm modern living room" -> link to Salon collection [Source: collections/salon]
- Fri (Facebook): Product walkthrough video (table) + promo code post -> CTA shop sale [Source: homepage]
- Sat (LinkedIn): Case study teaser: hospitality project — CTA request a quote [Source: homepage]

script: Hook (0–2s) : « Avant → Après : transformez un coin en écrin d'automne »
Beat 1 (2–6s) : montrer le meuble Bunting seul — plan fixe avant.
Beat 2 (6–12s) : Tip 1 — « Superposez plaids et coussins : mêlez laine et lin » (rapide montage).
Beat 3 (12–18s) : Tip 2 — « Jouez avec la lumière chaude : lampes basses et bougies » (insert bougie/lampes).
Beat 4 (18–24s) : Tip 3 — « Mixez bois + matières naturelles : osier, céramique, lin » (détails).
Reveal (24–28s) : plan après complet — coin cosy, textures et grain du bois mis en valeur.
Ask (28–30s) : « Commentez avec une photo, taggez @boisetchiffons ou utilisez #BoisEtChiffonsAutomne — dites si l’on peut repartager. »
slides: Plan large : salle à manger / coin salon centré sur la Table à manger rectangulaire 240 cm | Acacia Bunting — couches de textiles (plaids, coussins) et luminaires doux, palette ocre/brun/rouille.
Gros plan : veinage et finition de l'acacia en contraste avec une texture laine ou lin — détails tactiles et grain du bois.
Détail styling : assiette en céramique, bougie, petite déco posée sur le buffet bas 3 portes 3 tiroirs | Acacia Bunting — idées d'accessoires disponibles sur le site.
Ambiance tamisée : lampes basses, plaid en grosse maille, lumière chaude qui fait ressortir la patine du bois.
Invitation UGC : grille visuelle de petites photos d'intérieur (exemples utilisateur possibles) + overlay texte « Partagez votre coin cosy » et rappel CTA (tag/hashtag).
